prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: After reading all eight openings I move my first choice to magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene. It is the candidate with the broadest support (seven of eight members ranked it, five in their top five) and, more to the point, it has the structure I value: a simple, general mechanism (a long-wavelength moire potential that quenches kinetic energy) was predicted analytically in 2011 by Bistritzer and MacDonald, and the 2018 experiments by Jarillo-Herrero's group then showed correlated insulators and superconductivity where the theory said the bands should be flat. The idea has since spread to many van der Waals systems, so it is a mechanism and not just a material. Theory and experiment are tied together cleanly, the observation has been reproduced by many independent groups, and a three-name prize fits the credited record better than most alternatives on the shortlist. My own B011 (active-matter hydrodynamics) remains, in my view, a deep and underappreciated body of work, but I should be honest that it enters this round with a single supporter, me, and that a field-wide recognition of it has not formed on this committee.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity of understanding, which I care about more than reproducibility. The correlated-insulator and flat-band phenomenology is secure, but the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated, so a citation must be worded around the flat bands and correlated states and not claim an explanation of the superconductivity. The attribution is also not airtight: Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto identified flat-band physics in twisted bilayers earlier, and Cao, Fatemi and other members of the experimental team are not credited. If the committee judges that the early-theory record or the experimental co-first-author question cannot be settled, B012 or B049 are safer in terms of settled interpretation.

responses.point: Johansson ranks optical lattice clocks first as a clean, controllable quantum experiment in which every physical detail matters, with Katori proposing the magic-wavelength lattice and Ye taking it to record accuracy, and he ranks twisted bilayer graphene only fifth because the nature of its superconductivity is unsettled and he suspects it is slightly early.
responses.response: I take the maturity point seriously and share it as far as the superconducting mechanism goes, but I would separate the two things the prize would be for. The flat bands, the correlated insulator and the superconducting dome are reproduced across many groups; what is unsettled is the pairing glue, which was also true of cuprate superconductivity when it was recognised. The clock case is excellent on precision and on replication, but I ask what the essential new physical mechanism is: magic-wavelength trapping is a very clever way to cancel a systematic shift, whereas twisted bilayers revealed a previously unknown route to strong correlations. I would not rule out B049 as a part of a final configuration, but I do not see it as obviously stronger on discovery grounds, and a Katori-Ye prize also has to deal with the 2005 comb prize lineage that Kroll and Pearce raised.

responses.point: Kroll puts optical lattice clocks first and ultracold-atom lattices second, stresses that credit on the clocks looks reasonably settled, and for B012 prefers one theorist and two experimentalists (Bloch, Greiner, Zoller) while noting the 2001 and 2012 prizes mean it must be framed carefully around lattice simulation.
responses.response: I agree that B012 is highly mature, and I moved from my own opening trio (Bloch, Cirac, Zoller) to see his point: omitting Greiner is a real cost, since the Mott-insulator experiment and the microscope are the decisive demonstrations, and the Cirac and Zoller names also sit in Danielsson's and Pearce's proposals. That is exactly why I hesitate to make B012 my preferred option: the credit boundary on four people (Jaksch, Hansch, Esslinger, Kasevich could also be argued) is harder to defend than for B009, where one prediction paper and one experimental group stand out. I do agree with Kroll that if the committee wants an atomic-physics prize, the cleanest framing is quantum simulation of Hubbard physics, not general cold-atom control.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the IceCube neutrino discovery (Halzen alone) first as a discovery from nature that opened a new window on the universe, and he places twisted bilayer graphene second, noting that it created the moire field and has a direct confirm-by-experiment structure.
responses.response: I accept his description of B009 and appreciate that it is his second choice. On B047 I am the wrong person to judge the detector physics, but as a statistician I would raise the attribution concern he himself notes: a single name for a cubic-kilometre collaboration whose precursors AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND did essential groundwork is a hard prize to defend, and Pearce also flags that single name may under-represent early leadership. Since the supplied credit lists only Halzen, I would want to see what the committee can say about other leaders before treating B047 as a competitor to B009.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first because the flat-band prediction preceded the 2018 experiments, a theory-experiment link he values, and notes that the correlated and superconducting phases are widely reproduced even though the pairing mechanism is still debated.
responses.response: I agree and would use his framing as the basis of the citation: prediction first, then experiment. I would push back on one point only, namely whether the pre-2011 literature affects the Bistritzer-MacDonald priority. Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto found flat-band signatures in twisted bilayers earlier, and the committee should look at whether the magic-angle statement itself (a specific angle and a quantitative continuum model) is what is being credited, because that is what we can defend.

uncertainties: Whether the earlier Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto work, and the co-first-author roles of Cao, Fatemi and others, weaken the three-name B009 attribution enough to change the configuration.
Whether the unsettled pairing mechanism makes recognition of the superconductivity premature, so that the citation should rest on flat bands and correlated insulators.
Whether B012 can be given a defensible three-person split among Bloch, Cirac, Greiner and Zoller, given that Jaksch and others are also arguably central.

Whether the committee will give any weight to active-matter hydrodynamics (B011), which currently has no support from other members; I cannot judge whether this is a lack of familiarity or a considered view.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with any shortlisted candidate or credited name is apparent from my profile; none of the credited people on the shortlist appears among my frequent co-authors or institutional ties. Two disclosures for transparency: my own field is adjacent to B011 (I have written on machine learning for active matter), which is an intellectual bias in favour of that candidate and not a recusal issue, and I share the Gothenburg physics environment with Johansson and Olsson, with no specific collaboration with either.
